claims.text: The target high-entropy alloys are initially disordered solid solutions with inherent chemical disorder.
Integrating molecular-dynamics phonon-PDOS simulations with cluster-expansion modeling will enable more accurate prediction of ultralow phonon thermal conductivity in HEAs.
Molecular-dynamics simulations can be used to obtain the phonon density of states in the proposed workflow.
Cluster expansion combined with configurational sampling can quantify chemical short-range order.
Chemical short-range order in refractory HEAs varies with temperature and composition.
The extent and type of local chemical short-range order modulate phonon-scattering pathways.
Atomic-scale short-range-order variations alter local force constants.
Short-range-order-induced changes in local force constants increase phonon scattering and reduce phonon mean free path.
Increased phonon scattering and reduced phonon mean free path lower lattice thermal conductivity.
Explicitly representing short-range order will cause the integrated approach to predict lower phonon thermal conductivity than conventional approaches.
The integrated approach will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 20–30% relative to methods using MD or cluster expansion separately.
Existing baseline models use isolated MD phonon calculations or empirical correlations without accounting for short-range-order-induced scattering.
The proposed method is applicable to chemically disordered HEAs with predominantly BCC or FCC structures.
The method may lose accuracy in extremely off-stoichiometric systems.
The method may lose accuracy when precipitate formation dominates the microstructure.
The magnitude of the accuracy improvement and the temperature dependence of the short-range-order effects remain experimentally uncertain.
A benchmark can compare integrated-model predictions with measured lattice thermal conductivity across HEA compositions, annealing treatments, and temperatures.
The hypothesis is falsified if the integrated predictions have R2 below 0.7 against experimental thermal-conductivity measurements or fail to improve on conventional models.
